title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
extended_summary:
This reflection paper examines current debates and research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education, with a focus on how AI affects cognitive learning processes and outcomes. The authors argue that discussions around AI are often shaped by hype and overgeneralization, and they call for more evidence-based research that distinguishes between genuine learning gains and superficial performance improvements.

The paper proposes the ISAR model, which classifies AI effects on learning into four types: inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition. Using this framework, the authors synthesize prior research on AI-enhanced learning, including intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI, large language models, teacher-facing tools, and student-facing applications such as conversational agents, feedback systems, dashboards, and AI-generated instructional materials. They emphasize that AI can support learning when it augments instruction or enables deeper learning tasks, but it can also reduce learning if students over-rely on AI or if the tool design is poorly aligned with instructional goals.

The paper is not an empirical study of a specific population or intervention, but a conceptual review aimed at educators, researchers, and designers working in AI-enhanced education. It highlights that successful AI integration depends on student and teacher prerequisites such as AI literacy, pedagogical skill, and contextual factors like infrastructure and regulation. The main conclusion is that AI should be treated as an instructional support that must be carefully designed, validated, and used in ways that preserve cognitive engagement and human involvement.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI / large language model chatbot used for general-purpose text generation, question answering, and interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as a non-educational generative AI tool used in educational settings, and cites studies using it for student tasks such as scientific inquiry, writing revision, and support in learning activities. It is contrasted with educational AI systems and with teacher-facing uses of generative AI.

findings.finding_summary: In the cited study by Stadler et al. (2024), students used ChatGPT during a scientific inquiry task on nanoparticles in sunscreen. ChatGPT simplified task processing by reducing extraneous and intrinsic load, but this did not improve learning effectiveness and was accompanied by reduced cognitive processing depth and lower cognitive learning outcomes, as reflected in the quality of arguments in a posttest justification task.
findings.measure: Quality of arguments in a posttest justification task; cognitive processing depth (germane load)

findings.finding_summary: In the cited study by Fan et al. (2024), ChatGPT was compared with a human expert chat, writing analytics tools, and no support during a writing task. ChatGPT improved task performance during the supported intervention phase, but there were no differences in posttest knowledge gain or knowledge transfer; learners also showed relatively low metacognitive processing, which the authors characterized as possible 'metacognitive laziness'.
findings.measure: Task performance during supported intervention phase; posttest knowledge gain; knowledge transfer; metacognitive processing

quality_tier_rationale: This is a reflection/theoretical paper rather than a primary empirical evaluation of ChatGPT. The ChatGPT findings are reported secondhand from cited studies, without full methodological detail or direct effect estimates in this paper.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports both negative and mixed ChatGPT-related outcomes, including reduced learning effectiveness in one cited study and no posttest gains in another. Because effect sizes are not reported here and the evidence is indirect, the impact is best treated as modest/unclear overall.
